T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | M A Y 2 0 2 6
Focusing on
Form & Finishing
by Dimitri Harvalias
Prior to purchasing a lathe earlier this year, my experience with
wood turning included a bowl I turned 50 years ago in high
school, a one day bowl class, and an afternoon workshop on
pen turning.
I recently found this piece of Camphor burl in the offcuts bin
at KMS Tools for $10. I really liked the gentle swirling character
of the burl, but the blank had a chunk taken out of one side
limiting the potential size and shape for a bowl. I also wanted
to make a piece that used contrasting woods so I decided to
split the blank and insert some milled maple leftover from a
kitchen cabinet project to ‘extend’ the base and get a slightly
larger bowl from it.
I thought a simple cross
of the maple centered
on the bowl would be a
bit too static, so I offset
the cuts to either side
of center. I mounted
the blank using a worm
screw and began turning
the outside of the bowl.
I found the camphor cut
easily but the intermittent hardness of the maple compared to
the camphor made it difficult to cut evenly. I’m not sure if that
feeling was real or imagined but I eventually got more consis
tent with each pass.
The shavings were very aromatic and I saved a Ziploc bag full
of them to give to my mother. When she was a child in Greece
they used camphor in place of mothballs. As I was turning the
smell took me back to visits to my grandmother’s house in
Greece.
Sanding the piece was problematic as the fine dust created
from the camphor permeated the fibres of the maple, espe
cially in the end grain. Although not clearly visible initially,
as soon as finish was applied it caused noticeable streaks on
the lighter wood. A lack of patience led me to apply a finish of
mineral oil and beeswax without really solving the issue.
The initial piece I brought to the GVWG Instant Gallery had
some serious shortcomings. In addition to the staining of the
end grain, the bottom of the bowl sat clumsily on the table and
the inside was not hollowed deep enough, leaving the lower
part of the bowl very thick and heavy.
A few welcomed comments and suggestions from folks at the
Focus on Form and Finish table encouraged me to make some
adjustments. I refined the outside profile adding a gentle curve
through the mid-section and turned the top edge slightly
inward. I removed some material on the inside to make it
more consistent with the outside form which made the walls
thinner and reduced the visual and physical bulk of the piece.
I also took a bit of time to try and solve the staining issue and
refinished the bowl.
At this early stage in my turning journey, every time I step in
front of the lathe brings a new experience and an opportunity
to improve. My take-aways from this project are to resist the
rush to ‘get it finished’, and take more time to consider the
form.
Got a project you’d like to see featured in our newsletter?
Get in touch by email: editor@gvwg.ca

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | M A Y 2 0 2 6
President’s Message
by Don Gamble
Every so often, a month comes along that reminds us just
how wide the world of woodturning really is. This is one of
those months.
We’re welcoming Matt Monaco, whose work and teaching
focus on clean form, tool control, and the fundamentals that
make good turning feel effortless. If you’ve watched any of
his demonstrations or courses, you know how clearly he
breaks things down — stance, sharpening, tool presentation,
and the cuts that give you a clean surface right off the tool.
It’s a great reminder that solid fundamentals open the door
to everything else we do.
Later this year, we’re working to bring in Heather Marusiak,
whose work lives in a completely different creative universe.
Heather draws inspiration from the fossils and landscapes
of the Kansas Flint Hills, creating pieces that are turned,
carved, textured, and painted. She writes that she search
es for “a sense of self and a sense of place,” and her work
shows how far the lathe can take you once you step beyond
the circle. Her pieces prove that woodturning doesn’t have
to stop at round — it can become sculptural, layered, and
deeply personal.
What I love about having both of these artists in our orbit
is how clearly they show the range of our craft. From Matt’s
disciplined, classic forms to Heather’s carved and painted
explorations, there’s no single right way to be a woodturner.
As Richard Raffan once put it, “An indescribable surface
that begs for a caress of the hand — that’s what I think wood
should provide.” That applies whether the surface came
straight off a gouge or was carved, textured, or painted into
something entirely new.
So this month, I hope you’ll take a moment to explore a
corner of the craft you don’t usually visit. Try a new cut. Try
a new surface. Try a new idea. Bring it to the Instant Gallery
— successful or not. We learn the most when we share what
we’re experimenting with.
Our Guild is at its best when we celebrate the full spectrum
of what woodturning can be. And this year, with guests like
Matt and Heather, we get to see that spectrum in action.
See you at the meeting — and I can’t wait to see what you’re
working on.

15% Discount for GVWG Members
If you give the cashier your phone number, you will only get
the store 5% non-Guild discount. By saying GVWG instead you
get the 15% Guild discount.
If you are buying something that needs a warranty, just give
them your Name and Address and that will go on the electron
ic file. If the item you are buying has a flyer sale that is better
than the 15%, then you will automatically get the better rate.
Every purchase you make in the store by using this process
adds to our GVWG Credit account which we use to buy KMS
gift certificate prizes. We even bought our Laguna lathe for
Sapperton Hall with this! By doing this you are giving yourself
a better discount and helping the guild at the same time.
If you are an out-of-town Guild member, all you have to do is
type in GVWG as the customer name when buying, and type in
your full name, address etc. in the ‘ship-to’ field and you will
get the 15% discount.
The 15% is an average savings and is based on the cost mar
gins from that manufacturer. This does not apply to published
special flyer items. If we all do this, we can even get up to a
bigger discount level in future!

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | M A Y 2 0 2 6
Editor’s Notes
by Britchie
Hello everyone.
Our newsletter this month delivers a diverse range of articles
and interests—evidence of a very active and engaged Chap
ter (IMO).
The front cover features a bowl made by Dimitri Harvalias.
It’s a piece that I (and a number of other members) com
mented on for its understatement and competency of exe
cution—qualities made all the more impressive by the fact
that he acquired a lathe only in January this year. As it turns
out, Dimitri also participated in one of the new ‘Focus on
Form’ round table sessions. As a result, he made a number
of visual and ‘weight’ refinements to his piece while at the
same time, advancing his knowledge and appreciation of
this wonderful art form.
To say that Ed Pretty has written-up a few notes on his Guild
Night presentation would be a complete understatement!
In his follow-up article entitled “The ‘Secrets’ you Probably
Already Know”, Ed has put together a comprehensive article
detailing the fundamentals of lathe chisel cuts, catches,
approach angles, body posture and more.
We also have an article with a more international perspec
tive by Pippa Lattey. Pippa who now heads-up the Women
In Woodturning (WIT) group, writes about her recent trip
“down under” which included an artists residency and her
attendance of TURNFEST, Australia’s largest annual wood
turning event.
We have some great photos from the Spring “Intro to Bowl
Turning” class run by Claudia Hayward, assisted by Bob
Gilson.
Last but not least, there are more examples of member art
istry and industry in the Instant Gallery and the President’s
Challenge: “The Space Between”.
In finishing up, I wrote in the last issue regarding some
guidelines I’ve been working on for shaping our newsletter
content with the goal of “Raising the profile of our Chapter
within the AAW and wider community”.
Here’s the key elements of that objective:
•
Increasing author diversity (WIT, newcomers etc.)
•
Promoting artistry and industry
•
Fostering leadership in subject matter
•
Maximizing educational value
•
Encouraging participation
•
Elevating content presentation
As if by providence, the content submitted this month
seems to have already self-aligned with some of these...
Write me with your ideas or feedback: editor@gvwg.ca
Happy turning!

E D I T O R S ’ S N O T E S

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | M A Y 2 0 2 6
Being aware of the direction of the force exerted on
the tool by the rotating wood, how you control the
force that you apply to the tool and generally consid
ering the various things that impact the path of the
tool is the key to getting the result you are working
toward. Various “occurrences” at the lathe may seem
like a mystery but in some cases, you may already be
aware of the contributing factors, just not some of
the connective tissue. Have you ever found yourself
clenching, knowing that you are about to get a catch,
for instance? You know it’s coming but you don’t
know why. You just haven’t connected the dots yet.
Let’s try to put those dots together in an understand
able way.
I apologize in advance for the long read but there was
a tremendous amount of information packed into my
demo. Since “showing” is essentially pictures, and
each picture is worth a thousand words…
Catches
It’s fair to say that the fear of getting a catch is the
largest cause of stress and therefore hesitation and
uncertainty in woodturning. If you understand what
causes a catch, you are 95% of the way to preventing
them. There are two – only two – causes of catches.
The first occurs when addressing the wood with the
cutting edge first (photo 1). This can be intention
al or by accident. We know the tool wants to go in
the direction the bevel is pointing. In this case it’s
pointing into the wood so that’s where is goes – with
varying intensity. The solution is to address the wood
with the heel of the bevel (photo 2) then use that as

G U I L D M E M B E R A R T I C L E
The “Secrets”
you Probably
Already Know
by Ed Pretty
When we’re turning, all kinds of things hap
pen that cause outcomes, both good and
bad, that contribute to the final piece that
we are creating. Understanding why those
outcomes occur is what makes the differ
ence between an enjoyable experience or,
sadly, sometimes a stressful or even a fright
ening experience.
1

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | M A Y 2 0 2 6
a fulcrum to close the cutting edge onto the wood.
When you approach the wood with the tool, don’t try
to “nail it”. Emphasize the placement of the heel on
the wood.
The second – and the least understood – is when the
“support point” (contact point of the tool on rest) and
the “load point” (cutting edge on the wood) are not in
line with the rotational force at the point of contact.
That force is essentially vertical when cutting at the
9 o’clock position (just above center when turning a
bowl) on the wood. On a tool with a round shank (i.e.
bowl gouge), this can cause a rotational force on the
tool resulting in the cutting edge digging in progres
sively deeper as the wood rotates. In photo 3 you
can see that the downward force (chip on the cutting
edge) is not in line with the support point (bottom
of the tool on the rest), so will roll the tool into the
wood. This is also an issue with a skew since it is rest
ing on one corner on the tool rest. On a bowl gouge,
the indicator is the cutting point on the bowl gouge
is moving from the “bottom” of the flute to the “side”
or the wing on a bowl gouge (when the tool is held
roughly in a horizontal cutting position). On the skew,
if the cut occurs at about the middle third, life is good
(see photo 4 showing the support in line with the
force). If it moves toward the long point of the skew,
life is about to become bad (photo 5). In my book, a
bowl gouge catch makes a skew catch look like child’s
play, probably because it grabs a bigger chunk of the
pie.
To prevent the classic catch on the outside of the
bowl about 7/8 of the way toward the rim, keep the
flute open at about 45 degrees all the way around
the bowl (photos 6 & 7). This keeps the load point
and support point in line with the downward force.
For folks who simply stand at the lathe without using
their legs and body to drive the cut, the only way of
keeping the bevel in contact is to roll the tool open.
When the tool becomes close to being wide open
(looking straight down into the maw of the flute) the
cut is happening on the side of the wing and disaster
is about to strike (photo 8). The answer is to move
(Continued from the previous page)
(Continues on the next page)

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | M A Y 2 0 2 6
your body to keep that gouge open to no more than
45 degrees. More about that further on.
While on the subject of catches
Since we’re talking about the rotational force of the
work exerting a downward force on the tool, let’s talk
about entering a cut on the face of the work (we’re
talking bowls here but it’s the same in spindle turning
when using a gouge to cut a cove). When turning at
about center, the rotational force is basically vertical
at the point of contact with the face. If the very tip
of the tool is at an angle with that force, the tool will
tend to run in that direction. If the tool is vertical and
in line with the force, it will remain stable (photos 9 &
10). If leaning toward center it will go toward center,
if leaning toward the outside it will go toward the out
side (photo 11). The farther you are from center, the
greater the force. Understanding this, you will never
again ruin the rim on your almost-complete bowl. If
the tops of the flute are vertical (100% closed), the
tip is inline with the rotational force, and the tool will
remain stable.
To further enhance your control
Pushing the tool forward to start any cut offers no
control because you have no “brakes”. You generally
don’t have a lot of control over the speed of entry. To
have control over the “speed of entry” and also have
“brakes”, lower the tool into the work rather than
pushing the tool into the work. To do this, lower the
back of the tool significantly, place it very near the
surface of the work, anchor the tool on the rest then
(Continued from the previous page)
(Continues on the next page)
87
G U I L D M E M B E R A R T I C L E
7
8
9
10
6

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | M A Y 2 0 2 6
slowly raise the back of the tool. The tip will move
closer and enter the wood very slowly because you
have greater control over how fast you raise the tool
over a significantly longer distance. You can also stop
lifting at any time, therefore you have “brakes”. This
method will also buy you a lot of “fudge factor” if your
tool isn’t placed exactly correctly because it will cut
its way into the wood rather than shocking it. Person
ally, over time, this has become the way I start every
cut.
Your hands have different jobs
At a normal lathe (without a rotating headstock) when
turning a bowl, your left hand is typically forward and
your right hand is back. The power from your legs
to drive the tool forward should come through your
back hand driving the tool forward. The front hand’s
job is to steady the tool and absorb the vibration. The
added advantage is that the forward thrust along the
centerline of the tool aids in keeping the tool nicely
registered on the wood. Using the forward hand to
power the tool tends to relieve that pressure causing
chatter or even steering the tool out of the cut.
To do this, it’s wise to hold the tool with your left
hand in such a way that it’s impossible to pull the
tool. I usually pinch the tool (because you have to
pull the tool to enter a cut: see below) with my thumb
and forefinger then morph that into a position where
they are simply resting on the wings of the flute. If
your fingers are “behind” the tool, it’s almost a cer
tainty that you will pull the tool (photo 12). Experi
ment in air off the rest. If your grip is such that you
can pull the tool, then you will do that on the work.
Try to find a grip that works for you.
Of course there is always an exception. To drive the
tool forward with the back hand requires that the tool
is on the wood so that the bevel can direct the tool
forward. When you are off the wood at the start of a
cut, of course you need to engage the rest with your
forward hand then draw the tool into the wood with
that hand. Once the bevel is on the wood, simply roll
your hand away from the rest and carry on.
This is valuable information for left handers because
the natural thing is to power your tool with the dom
inant (forward) hand. Not doing this is difficult I am
sure, but at least knowing there is an issue is a start.
Most left-handers have adapted to many things in this
right-handed world so sometimes it’s not so difficult.
If it is a significant problem, an alternative is to get a
lathe with a rotating headstock or a sliding headstock
to work off the end of the lathe. This will allow you to
place your right hand forward and your left hand at
the back where it can do the most good.
A common left-handed (left back/right forward) cut is
when making a seriously heavy cut on the outside of
a bowl. In this case you are using both hands to drive
the tool into the cut and forward. It’s a viable tech
nique but not typically used when making most cuts.
If you’re a spindle turner (Yay!), handedness is a
non-issue. It’s only those needy bowl turners who
have to deal with this. (I hope you know I’m kidding).
It’s a tool rest, not a tool guide
I see many turners engaging the tool with their for
ward hand at all times. So much so, that they may
(Continued from the previous page)
(Continues on the next page)

G U I L D M E M B E R A R T I C L E
12
11

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | M A Y 2 0 2 6
have to be surgically removed. I believe this comes
from the aforementioned uncertainty which is prob
ably from experiencing some pretty scary catches.
Clearly there are times when you need to engage
the tool rest with your forward hand – but there are
also times when doing so is a huge impediment. So
how do we decide? The cutting edge always needs
support, so: A) When the cutting edge does not have
support from the wood, engage the rest with your
forward hand. B) When the cutting edge does have
support from the wood, do not engage the tool rest
with your hand. What this boils down to is “trust the
bevel” to get the tool to go where you want it to go.
In reality, it’s more like “trust yourself”. We all under
stand that the bevel controls the direction of the cut,
so let it do its job.
By engaging the tool rest with your front hand while
making a cut, a couple counterproductive things hap
pen. First, the power provided by the back hand is of
ten reduced or negated by dissipating that force into
the tool rest instead of the wood. This is a common
cause of chatter. Secondly, if the hand is engaging the
rest, you have to devise some alternative method of
“getting around the corner” on the outside of a bowl.
The same thing happens if your hand is hanging down
and eventually runs into the tool rest.
I have heard people say to use the tool rest to make a
straight cut. That works only if, A) you set is correctly
and B) it’s a straight cut. What do you do if it’s a taper
or there is a curve involved? I can’t say it enough:
Trust The Bevel! I produce straight rollers for a cus
tomer and have developed an effective way of making
a straight, axial cut. They have to be within 0.015”
(1/64”) on each end. Size your piece at both ends (and
the middle if a long cut), start making your cut from
one end but aim the bevel high (make the diameter
progressively larger and larger). With each successive
cut, aim the bevel lower and lower until you reach
the desired diameter at the other end. Remember
to use your whole body to power the tool. Standing
soldier-like will not get the job done.
Opening the flute
From my experience with years with students, right
out of the gate, about 50% naturally do this operation
correctly and 50% incorrectly. I watch and if they do it
correctly, I reference it later for the record. The other
half I deal with it right away. You will be in one of
these groups.
This seems insignificant but it makes enough differ
ence at the start of the cut that if you roll the tool
open incorrectly, you end up with a vase instead of a
platter.
Imagine there is a wire running through the center
line of the tool. Rotate the tool around that axis.
While opening the flute causes some altering in the
position of the contact point of the bevel (ultimate
ly, the direction it’s going to go), the “wrist up/wrist
down” (or forearm up/forearm down) motion keeps
that change to a minimum.
A “hand up/hand down” motion while the forearm
remains fixed produces greater a swinging/sweep
ing motion at the tip causing significantly more of a
change in bevel angle to the wood. This often makes
a huge change in the direction at the very start of the
cut resulting in difficulty achieving the desired form.
To visualize what I just described as the correct mo
tion, loosely grip the tailstock quill. Rotate your hand
up and down as if opening the flute on a gouge and
you will see that the hand rotates around the center
line while the wrist and forearm move up and down.
One nice plus when doing this is to let your forward
hand come up with the tool as you open the flute.
This will lift your paw above the tool rest so it won’t
get in the way when “going around the corner”.
Using your whole body while turning, not just your
arms and hands
Under “Catches”, I noted that the “open flute” catch is
a result of standing soldier-like at the lathe and trying
to turn the outside of the bowl form without using
your legs. This is the solution: when you have to trav
el any distance (all bowl cuts and long barrel shapes
in spindle turning), you will find you need to use your
whole body more than just your arms.
(Continued from the previous page)
(Continues on the next page)
89
G U I L D M E M B E R A R T I C L E

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | M A Y 2 0 2 6
Making a forward cut with locked knees can only
be done by rotating your upper body at some point
which results in the cutting edge making an arcing
path centered around your body core. This results in
unwanted form, chatters or constantly coming out of
the cut. Or all of the above.
Bend your knees to the point that you feel your quad
muscles (more the right at the start of a cut) support
the weight of your body, point your right toe slightly
in the direction of the cut so that your ankle and knee
will work together. Push yourself into the cut from the
ball of your right foot, transferring your weight steadi
ly to the left foot. As the cut progresses, you should
feel your weight transfer to your left foot. Rotating
your upper body at the hips changes the angle of the
bevel to the wood, which in turn creates the desired
form as it moves forward in the cut.
Foot placement should be so that your weight is
almost entirely on the right foot at the start of the cut
and almost entirely on the left foot at the end of the
cut. Your cut, then, is simply a transfer of weight from
right foot to left foot. Your cut has ended when your
left knee is over your left toe. Any further and you
will be off balance and in danger of really messing up
the form. Everyone learns differently so occasionally
I have suggested “just move your left knee forward”
and that gets things coming together.
During this whole exercise, it really helps to firm up
your core, making your whole upper body one unit.
Never take a step with your left foot during the cut.
Instead, stop the cut and reposition. Making a “fake
cut” prior to a cut to see if your left foot can be
moved slightly to get a longer cut is a good practice.
If you can’t make the whole cut, acknowledge that
and make two cuts.
Using your quad muscles (legs) rather than your
smaller arm muscles results in far more control, plus
the ability to make a super-slow (meaning super con
trolled) cut, yet under full power. You won’t get nearly
as tired, either.
A good rule of thumb for foot placement when turning
the outside of a bowl (doesn’t work on the inside) is
roughly parallel to the tool rest. Parallel to the lathe
when making in-line cuts, 90° fore and aft to the lathe
when making crosscuts (facing) and about 45° when
making curved cuts.
To illustrate the power and control that you have
when using your large quad muscles, picture yourself
at a door with a heavy spring closer. Brace yourself
and try to open the door smoothly using just your
right arm (back hand when turning). Likely the effort
will result in an initial lunge and then smooth move
ment. Now try putting your shoulder against the door
and using your legs to power it open. You will find you
can open it smoothly and as slowly as you want. If,
when you are turning, your cuts have a lunge-lungelunge motion, you’re using only arm power. Your tool
is probably dull, too.
Where do you look when making a cut?
I’ve been turning for over 65 years and I still can’t
take my eyes off the shavings coming off the tool – it’s
just so cool – so I understand the urge to watch those
shavings. But when it comes to the “money shot”, my
eyes are on the horizon on the top of the bowl on the
outside and the opposite side of the cut on the inside.
But where on the horizon? If you watch the “step” of
the cut only that’s not much different than watching
the shavings. You need to see the big picture, essen
tially extrapolating the curve, trying to determine if
it’s heading where you want it to go. Look ahead of
the cut, just like looking across a curve when driving.
This may sound difficult, but it becomes surprising
ly natural very quickly. Just like driving a car: look
where you want to go.
Thoughts on scraping (above and below center)
I was initially taught to scrape on center. Smack-dab
on center, not higher, not lower. Both inside and out.
After several years of getting scraper catches, I decid
ed to figure it out for myself. Basically, it’s all about
“where will the tool go if it digs in”?
Follow the logic:
1. When scraping on the outside of a form, stay at
center (good) or slightly below (better). In the
(Continued from the previous page)
(Continues on the next page)
810
G U I L D M E M B E R A R T I C L E

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | M A Y 2 0 2 6
event of a catch the tool will swing into air, away
from the wood.
2. When scraping the inside of a form, stay above
center so that in the event of a catch the tool will,
again, swing into air, away from the wood.
3. When doing the “bottom” of the inside, clearly you
need to get to center on occasion. Unless you are
working with a very vase-like form, if the tool digs
in there is no wood below to cause a problem.
Upward sweep
Rather than maintaining a 9 o’clock position through
out your inside cut, try sweeping upward through
most of the cut then arcing down to center. This pro
duces an acute shear angle to the wood (read: cuts
way nicer). Generally, sweep upward through what
you would consider the “side” of the bowl and arcing
down in what you would consider the “bottom” of the
bowl. This creates a cut with greater shear (evident
from the nicer shavings), makes a cleaner cut and
I feel it helps the cutting edge last longer. Way less
effort, too.
Pull cut - bevel on the wood
What most turners consider a pull cut with the tool
held horizontally is not a controlled cut, because the
bevel is not on the wood. It is a peeling cut, useful in
removing large amounts of wood that you don’t want,
however there is not the level of control needed when
refining a form. When the tool is held horizontally,
the only way to not get a severe catch is to partially
open the flute enough to get that peeling cut but not
so far as to be scraping. Allowing the bevel to contact
the wood in this case is a guaranteed catch (and a
whopper at that).
Because you are using the wing (side) of the cutting
edge, the only way to make a pull cut with bevel
control is to align the tool with the direction of the
rotational force at the point of contact. This usually
means an almost vertical position of the tool with the
handle pointing toward the floor. In this way the load
point and support point are in line with the force,
causing no rotational action in the tool. As always,
engage the heel of the bevel, close the gap to the
cutting edge then proceed with the cut.
Parting thoughts
As in most things, there is always more than one
way to skin a cat, so different techniques than I have
described may achieve the same result as long as
you are considering all the forces. What I am trying to
describe is the dynamics that affect the tool on the
wood. As long as you understand that, it is possible to
achieve a result in a variety of ways.
There are exceptions to every “rule”. Also, if you know
and understand a rule, you will know how and when
you can break or bend it. You will develop ways to
get around problems by understanding what causes
things to happen – or not happen – as the case may
be. That takes time standing at the lathe. So go out
and turn as often as you can, always experiment and
ask yourself, “Why did/didn’t that happen?”
Don’t forget the one thing I mentioned during the
demo: everything in woodturning is “Goldie Locks”.
Not too hard, not too soft, not too fast, not too
slow, etc., etc. So much about woodturning has to
be “just right” and that feeling comes with time. But
take heart, it isn’t always a long time. Just the right
amount of time.

YOUR PERSONAL SAFETY
Always wear Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) such as
approved safety glasses or goggles that include side protec
tors. Use a full face shield for larger bowl, vessel, or any turning
involving chucks and faceplates. Wear a dust mask or an air
filtration helmet in conjunction with proper ventilation and/or
a dust collection system as appropriate. Remember—it’s the
fine airbourne particles that are harmful to your respiratory
system. Wear hearing protection during extended periods of
turning.
Tie back long hair and avoid long sleeves or loose clothing.
Remove rings and other jewelry, or any dangling objects that
may catch on rotating parts or accessories.
Stay alert. Watch what you are doing. Pay close attention to
unusual sounds or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the
cause. Don’t operate machines when you are tired or under
the influence of drugs or alcohol.
WORKING SAFELY WITH YOUR LATHE
Ensure your workpiece is securely fastened. When using a
faceplate, be certain the workpiece is solidly mounted with
stout screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws as a minimum).
Do not use drywall or deck screws. When turning between
centers, check the workpiece is firmly mounted between the
headstock and tailstock and rotate your workpiece forwards/
backwards by hand to make sure it clears the toolrest and bed
before turning the lathe on.
Check all locking devices on the tailstock and tool rest as
sembly (rest and base) are tight before operating the lathe.
Check the speed of your lathe BEFORE turning it on. Use
slower speeds for larger diameters or rough pieces and higher
speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced.
Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is
balanced. If the lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the speed.
If the workpiece vibrates, always stop the machine to under
stand why. As a starting point, consult your operator’s manual
for recommended speeds for a particular lathe. Ensure the
lathe speed is compatible with the diameter of the blank.
Stay clear of danger zones directly behind and in front of the
workpiece. They are the most likely areas for a piece to travel
as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of
this zone when turning on the lathe, keeping your hand on the
switch in case you need to turn the machine off. When observ
ing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
Turn the lathe off before adjusting anything including the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
Always remove chuck keys, adjusting wrenches, and knock
out bars immediately after use. Never leave them in place,
even for a moment. Always remove the tool rest before sand
ing, finishing, or polishing operations.
Know your capabilities and limitations. An experienced
woodturner is capable of lathe speeds, techniques, and proce
dures not recommended for beginning turners.
Exercise extra caution when using stock with cracks, splits,
checks, bark pockets, knots, irregular shapes or protuberanc
es. Beginners should avoid these types of stock until they have
greater knowledge of working such wood.
Hold turning tools securely on the toolrest, holding the tool
in a controlled but comfortable manner. Always contact the
tool rest with the tool before contacting the wood.
Never work with a lathe in reverse unless the chuck is using
a locking set-screw. It is possible for a chuck or faceplate to
unscrew unless it is fitted securely on the lathe spindle.
Don’t overreach. Keep proper footing and keep your balance

You mostly work on your own so safety is
YOUR responsibility. Please take the time to
read our safety guidelines and make them part
of your daily turning practice. Be safe out there!

at all times.
Keep tools sharp and clean for better and safer performance.
Don’t force a dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose for which
it was not designed or intended.
Consider your work environment. Don’t use a lathe in damp
or wet locations. Do not use in presence of flammable liquids
or gases, and always keep a fully-charged fire extinguisher
close at hand. Keep your work area well lit.
Guard against electric shock. Inspect electric cords for dam
age. Avoid the use of extension cords.
Never leave a lathe running unattended. Turn power off.
Don’t leave lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
SAFETY MAINTENANCE
Keep your lathe in good repair. Ensure belt guards or protec
tive covers are in place. Check for damaged parts, alignment,
binding of moving parts, and other conditions that may affect
its operation.
Read and follow safety guidelines for your lathe and other
workshop equipment. Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially bandsaws and chainsaws.

Woodturning Photography Guidelines (How to elevate the presentation of your work)
•
For general shots, leave some space around your piece when photographing (It’s easy to crop-in but very time consuming to
add space).
•
Backgrounds: try to use a plain backdrop and one that is big enough to fill the scene. A large sheet or preferably a roll that
curves from horizontal to vertical is ideal.
•
Image requirements: 1K - 3K pixels is adequate @300 pixels per inch. PSD, JPG, PNG formats.
•
Camera vs Phone: modern phone lenses are more than adequate for general product shots (be mindful of fish-eye effects on
the periphery). If you’re taking shots for galleries or print publications, use a camera.
•
Lighting: Get some help to set-up lighting in a repeatable fashion. As a backstop, you can photograph outside on a bright but
overcast day.
•
Composition: Experiment with some different angles and/or groupings of your work

Down Under
at TURNFEST
Australia
by Pippa Lattey
In March I attended Turnfest, Australia’s biggest wood
turning event. I went to the AAW Symposium in Portland
in 2024, and I was looking to attend another another
symposium, but not in the US. I picked Turnfest and
worked it into a bigger trip to Australia, including an
artist residency and a visit with my mom in Brisbane.
Turnfest is organized by David Drescher, owner of
South East Queensland Woodworking Supplies. Tick
et price includes accommodation and meals. It takes
place at the Seaworld resort, which is on a spit with a
surf beach across the road... but I didn’t make it over for
a swim. During the three days I spent there, I kept very
busy.
We started on Friday morning, with unstructured demos
and a Tool Shop. I saw Simon Begg turn a sphere from
Camphor Laurel, filling the room with a fresh scent.
I also caught the end of a segmented pen demo with
first-time demonstrator Katie Richer.
At 11am, we all squeezed into a large room for opening
remarks, with David introducing the demonstrators and
the “overseas” guests, including myself, one American,
and several from the UK. There were also many from
New Zealand, and right across Australia. Then we all
walked over to the restaurant for the first of many buffet
meals (including local prawns!). I tried to sit with differ
ent folks at each meal, but I especially connected with
some folks from Perth, and a father and daughter from
Melbourne: the youngest attendee, celebrating their
17th birthday at Turnfest. Everyone was friendly and
wanted to chat with “the Canadian”.
Interesting Demographics: Women
The demographics seemed more varied than in Port
land (or in the GVWG). I was happy to see there were
many more women. Most women I met were there on
their own, not with their partners. Before I arrived, I was
a little unsure. I knew there was a Craft Room setup for
the “ladies”, but I did not bring along my knitting be

cause I was there for the turning! However, Emma Cook
encouraged me to check it out, and I enjoyed connect
ing with the women there. They were serious makers,
and it was good to sit around and chat about making.
I learned about other Australian turning events, where
folks show up with their caravans (RVs) and their lathes
and hang out for a few days. I also connected with Sha
ron and Jim McConnachie from far North Queensland.
Jim is a legend, and we had a good chat about the
woods in his segmented turnings, which all come from
trees on his property.
Each room had a profes
sional videographer and two

view and one moving). The
lathes were all Vicmarc.
There were bandsaws in
some of the rooms, and I was

With no online attendees,
and a smaller audience, there was no need to “repeat
the question”, so discussions flowed smoothly. I tried
to catch each demonstrator once, but I was starstruck
by Emma Cook, and attended two of her demos.
Instant Gallery
There was an “Instant Gallery” with a wide range of
pieces made with Australian woods. The Neil Scobe
prize went to Nikki Phillips for a piece of pyrography,
a portrait of an Aborigine man with a spear, which felt
culturally awkward to me. We were all surprised that the
pyrography won, as she also created a delicately carved
‘ribbony’ hollow form which was a real crowd pleaser.
At the final lunch on Sunday they raffled off the demo
pieces, and I was thrilled to take home a teeny tiny
skew by Colwin Way (from his Taming of the Skew
demo). I also came away with a mild case of Covid, as
there was an outbreak at the resort. Still, it was worth
it!
Brisbane Woodturner’s Society
I stayed in Brisbane for a few
weeks after Turnfest (though
I missed some action due to
the Covid). I visited the Bris
bane Woodturners twice: for
a weekly Tuesday meeting
+ pyrography session, and
then for a carving group.
They have an incredible per
manent home, a two-storey
building that was a Scout Hall and then a Men’s Shed,
before they moved in. On the main floor is a space for
meetings and demonstrations, a big room full of lathes
and grinders, a side space packed with turning tools,
a small kitchen, a library, and a store. Downstairs is a
full wood shop and a whole lot of wood storage. New
Guinea Rosewood and Jacaranda are probably the most
popular, but there are also many Eucalyptus. All of their
woods are HARD, starting around Oak hardness and
goes up from there. The Brisbane Woodturner’s Society
makes hundreds of wood toys for charity each year.
They have a toy making group, a box making group, a
pyrography group, and a carving group that meet there
regularly.

This Spring’s Intro to Bowl Turning Class took place in late
April with 5 enthusiastic participants. Everyone had some
previous experience on the lathe. The primary objective of the
class is to give participants the skill and confidence to safely
make controlled cuts with the gouge and by the end, all were
able to handle their tools more comfortably. We talked tools,
sharpening, form, tenons, sanding, finishing and a myriad of
questions that came up. By the end of the third day, everyone
felt more confident and were grateful to have had an oppor
tunity to have so many blanks to practice on. Many thanks to
Brian and many others in the background who help to make
this course a success!
